item.title: Abusive pensions initiative: the situation in Switzerland
item.description: The popular initiative 'Yes to protection against illegal rents' collected 108,437 valid signatures. Here's what's changing for Swiss tenants.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Reached 108,437 valid signatures for the popular initiative. - The initiative aims to combat rents defined as abusive. - Calculated an average surcharge of CHF 360 per month per tenant. - The proposal now goes to the Federal Council and Parliament.
## Key facts - **What**: 'Yes to protection against abusive rents' initiative - When: Confirmation of success today - Where: Switzerland - Who: Swiss Tenants Association and Yannick Demaria - Amount: 360 francs average monthly surplus - Volume: 10.6 billion francs total surplus
The Federal Chancellery has officially certified the success of the popular initiative called 'Yes to protection against illegal rentals'. With 108,437 signatures declared valid, the text continues its institutional process, reaching the tables of the Federal Council and Parliament. The resulting political debate touches closely on the majority of residents in Switzerland, in a context where housing is an essential need. The initiative does not merely raise a question of principle, but is based on detailed economic calculations prepared by the BASS institute under the mandate of the Swiss Tenants' Association. The central figure that emerged concerns an average surplus of 360 francs per month for each rental dwelling, a figure that on an annual basis exceeds 4,300francs. Altogether, the volume of these surpluses is estimated at CHF 10.6 billion. The analysis of the current mechanism highlights how the protection system is based on the initiative of the individual. The structure of the market, where the landlord often holds an advantageous position, makes it difficult for the tenant to challenge the rent without risking complex procedures. The initiative proposes a redefinition of 'abusive rent', strictly linking it to the actual management costs and the purchase price of the property. This transformation is not aimed at denying the owners a return, but at limiting the speculation that occurs in changes of tenant. In recent years, pressure from the real estate lobby has manifested itself through proposals aimed at facilitating cancellations, perceived by tenants as attempts to weaken existing guarantees. Each time a tenant leaves the apartment, the landlord has the opportunity to increase the rent, fueling a spiral of cost growth. The proposed regulatory amendment intends to intervene precisely on these dynamics, relieving individual citizens of the burden of having to independently demonstrate the iniquity of the fee. ### The impact on the cost of living. The issue is not only about the balance at the end of the month, but directly affects the possibility of maintaining one's social network and living close to one's workplace or children's schools. When rents increase uncontrollably, entire sections of the population are forced to move away from the centres
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). For those living or working in Switzerland, the evolution of this initiative represents a moment of reflection on how the right to housing is protected by institutions. Currently, those who reside in rental properties must refer to the provisions of the Code of Obligations to contest a rent deemed excessive. It is essential to understand that, in the absence of new laws, the procedure remains the responsibility of the tenant. To delve into one's financial situation, it is possible to consult tools such as the [salary calculator](nav:calculator), which allows for monitoring the impact of fixed expenses on the family budget. The current procedure requires verifying whether the rent is higher than what is justified by management costs and the permitted return, an operation often complex without the support of specialists. The initiative aims to simplify this framework by introducing periodic checks that would eliminate the need for citizens to pursue legal action in isolation. ### Guidance tools. Beyond the issue of rents, managing a family budget in Switzerland involves various expense items, such as health insurance premiums or social contributions. Housing remains, however, a central pillar: affordable housing allows for better long-term savings planning, for example through the [third pillar](nav:pillar3), which is fundamental for supplementing the AVS/LPP pension income. The initiative does not claim privileges, but asks for the respect of a principle of contractual fairness. Anyone in a situation of uncertainty regarding their rent can monitor the developments of this initiative through the official channels of the Confederation. Pending the examination by the Federal Council and the eventual parliamentary debate, it remains essential to stay informed about current provisions. ## Key facts - **What**: Recommendation to reject the Compass Initiative. - When: Decision in principle confirmed on Wednesday. - Where: Bern, Federal Council. - Who: Federal Council, Parliament, initiative promoters. - Amount: Over 111,000 valid signatures delivered.
The Federal Council has officially recommended to Parliament to reject the so-called "Compass Initiative", without advancing any counter-proposal, neither direct nor indirect. The decision, matured and reiterated last Wednesday on the basis of an orientation already consolidated on 26 November last year, marks a clear break point between the Executive and the promoters of the initiative. Thelatter, launched in 2024 and deposited in 2025 with the support of over 111,000 valid signatures, proposes to modify the constitutional rules relating to the process of approving international treaties. In particular, the text aims to impose a mandatory referendum for all agreements that provide for the transposition of rules of law. This mechanism, which requires a double majority of the people and Cantons, would be applied as a priority to future packages of agreements with the European Union, known The analysis of the practical implications regarding the rejection of the 'Bussola' Initiative reveals a deep conflict between the need for greater direct democratic participation and the necessity of maintaining efficient governance in international relations. The promoters' proposal is not limited to a procedural change, but touches the very essence of managing international treaties that have a direct impact on the cost of living and the labor market in Switzerland. Had the initiative been accepted, every future normative international agreement would have undergone a much more burdensome and uncertain ratification process. For the citizen, this would mean periodically facing calls to the polls with qualified majorities, making the negotiation of long-term agreements extremely complex. The Government fears that such a constraint would turn every agreement, even technical ones, into a field of total political confrontation, paralyzing diplomatic activity. From the perspective of economic stability, the Federal Council's choice to favor the optional referendum allows for better management of the transposition of European regulations that influence key sectors such as the free movement of persons or the recognition of professional qualifications. The major concern relates to the transitional provision included in the text of the initiative, which specifically and targetedly aims to block or condition the approval of the EU package. ### Future scenarios and legislative impact If Parliament were to follow the Government's recommendation and reject the text, the current ratification practice would be confirmed. Apprenticeship in the Canton of Bern is a cornerstone of the Swiss education system, combining practical training in the company and theoretical lessons in vocational schools. With over 200 recognized professions, the Bernese dual system offers structured pathways regulated by the Federal Law on Vocational Training (LFPr) and cantonal regulations. ### Salary and living costs Progressive pay partially covers the costs of food, accommodation and educational materials. A first-year apprentice in an industrial company typically receives CHF 600-800 net monthly (after AVS/AI deductions). To compare purchasing power, the average cost of a shared room in Bern is CHF 750/month (UST 2025 data). Apprentices under the age of 25 benefit from reduced compulsory health insurance premiums (LAMal), with cantonal benefits of up to 50% for incomes below CHF 35'000 per annum.

For accommodation, the "Woko" service of the UIMP means between apprentices and landlords, guaranteeing reduced security deposits (maximum 2 monthly payments, as per the Code of Obligations).
### Transition to the labour market The employment rate of CFC graduates in the Canton of Bern is 92% within 6 months of completion (SECO 2024). 45% continue their studies, mainly in the SUP.
